title: Peace with God (Romans 5:1–11)
hookLine: suffering, patience, character, hope; while we were still sinners, Christ died

lines: HOW DID THEY GET THAT WAY?
cards: Ask the steady one in your life how they got that way, the one people call at two in the morning. The answer is rarely: everything went well for me. More often it's: the year my dad was sick.
The job I lost. The long winter after the divorce. Something hard happened, and something grew in the hard ground.
Nobody chooses the hard part, but what grew is often what they'd keep. Paul knew this from the inside: shipwrecked, beaten, jailed, and still writing letters.
In Romans chapter five he traces the pattern step by step, and he starts somewhere surprising: with peace.

teach.b: Chapter five opens, in the King James Bible: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."

The Greek word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting, but wholeness, everything in its right place. After four chapters about guilt and grace, the war is over.
He says we glory, even boast, in tribulations.

Not because suffering is good, but because of what can grow in it: "tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed." Four links. Hard times grow endurance.

Endurance grows what the King James calls experience; the Greek means tested character, like metal that's been through the fire and proved true. That tested character grows hope, and hope, Paul says, doesn't let you down.
Maketh not ashamed echoes Paul's opening a few days ago: not ashamed. Why doesn't it disappoint? Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts.
Then the line that holds the chapter up: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not after we got better.
While. Paul notes that hardly anyone would die even for a righteous person. This love didn't wait for anyone to deserve it.
Some readers say the chain is easier to see looking back than from the middle of it.

how: Christians often turn to Romans 5:1–5 in illness or loss; chaplains and friends read it with people in a hard season, and look back together on what that season grew.

o: a truce that lasts while you behave
a calm feeling during quiet prayer
wholeness, the war over, all in its place

games.q: what's inside the chain — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says suffering is good in itself
he glories in tribulation because of what can grow in it: patience, tested character, hope.
the word the King James calls experience means tested character
like metal that's been through the fire and proved true.
in Romans 5, God's love waits until people become good
"while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."

games.q: you're Paul, writing from a life of shipwrecks and beatings. how do you talk about suffering to a church you've never met?
o: tell them to avoid it at all costs.
say you glory in it, for what it grows.
tell them it's a punishment for sin.
games.why: Paul says "we glory in tribulations also", because tribulation works patience, then tested character, then hope, and hope makes not ashamed.

practice: Go back through your life slowly and find one hard season that, looking back, grew something in you: patience, compassion, honesty, a friend you'd never have met.
Don't pretend it was good, it may still hurt; just name the hardship and what grew, and if one you're in right now comes instead, let it be there without forcing a lesson on it yet.
If you pray, give thanks for what grew, and ask for hope in what hasn't yet.

wordCard.voice: Eirene. Paul's Greek word for peace, carrying the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, the war over, everything in its right place.

orig.note: Greek: peace. in the Bible it carries the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, all in its right place.
